questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I started my studies I always knew I wanted to go abroad for a semester. Choosing Spain was a combination of wanting to see life at an European Hospital different from Denmark (differences and similarities), explore a different culture, learning spanish and the thing that convinced my most of all to go to Spain was the previous students great recommendations.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think the emails I received from both universities would be a little confusing at some point and I had a bit of difficulties knowing exactly what to do when, but then I just wrote to the universities for help and they were both very helpful, so I wish I had just done that sooner.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Only communication through e-mail. The receiving at the hospital was very poor and when I finally found the person in charge of my stay at the hospital he only spoke spanish, so it was a bit difficult to understand everything for me.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I could have wished for more information regarding my stay upon arrival and maybe someone welcoming me and showing me around at the hospital the first day and getting me in contact with the other medical Erasmus students in Hospital de Cabueñes. That would have been very nice.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found my apartment on Airbnb. I could get a pretty good price for it when I rented it for 3 months+ and that meant I paid the same as I do for my apartment in Copenhagen each month. I was there with my boyfriend, but if I had been there alone, I would have preferred living with other students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I belive campus would be in Oviedo, but the placement of the hospital is in Gijón, so the commute is a bit long, so I think it would be easiest to live in Gijón.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I liked living in my apartment, but I think it would have been difficult for me to find housing in other ways. I would have tried to get one through a Facebook page maybe, there is one for each semester/year "ERASMUS GIJON" and then the year

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I was a little confused at first and found it difficult finding the hospital departments, but ended up finding it on wikipedia. Hospital de Cabueñes has a lot of different departments, so it was a good opportunity to try out fields that you are thinking about specializing in and maybe have not been able to try at your host university. I chose 4 different departments and was able to be at them all. And again if in doubt it is easiest to just write and ask.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was difficult to find the information, but I usually got all of my questions answered if I just wrote an email and asked.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the four specialities I wanted to try.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Find the departments in wikipedia and just ask if you can go to the departments you found interesting. I did four different specialities, which meant one for three weeks, and I found that suitable.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It depended on the department and the doctor how much they taught you doing the day, but overall I thought most doctors wanted you to learn, and made an effort in explaining and letting you do the examination. I also got to do a bone marrow sample at hematology, which was fun to try and I felt very safe during it with great supervision.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Final semester

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I did not have any classes, but I thought the doctors overall did a great job explaining and including me. The only time this didn't happen was when they were too busy or my spanish was just not good enough and their english also not good enough

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
12 weeks clinical rotation
- 3 weeks in internal medicine
- 3 weeks in hematology
- 3 weeks in pediatrics
- 3 weeks in neurology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend hematology, they were the nicest doctors to be with and I felt more included than anywhere else in the hospital.
Pediatrics was very hard for me to stay in because my spanish wasn't good enough for them and I didn't feel included at all, but maybe it would have been different if my spanish was better

Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *

Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Especially drinks were far less expensive than in Denmark. The apartment was a bit more expensive, than I could have hoped for, but overall everything was less expensive than in Denmark

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus Team planned a tapas party each thursday night, which I can highly recommend. At first I thought people were a bit young and very crazy party people, but after giving it a second chance I met amazing people, which I wished I had gotten to know sooner. Also they planned hiking trips, volleyball tournaments and a trip to Ibiza.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go surfing! You can rent a board and/or take classes. "Skool Surf" even has a danish-speaking instructor

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Rent a car (around 66 euro for a day) and drive out to explore beautiful Asturias, like the small town Cudillero (!) and Lastres, and the amazing mountains Picos de Europa.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The opening hours in the shops and restaurants are very different, because they close down doing the siesta, which was a bit hard to get used to, but once I did, I really enjoyed taking naps. Also people don't go out to eat until 21-22, but it wasn't a problem as soon as you got used to it.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Go to "Jueves de Tapas", the tapas party on thursdays in Gijón. The event is on the Erasmus Gijón-Facebook page. It can be a little intimidating at first, but it was a great way to meet people.
Also I would recommend to write to the person in charge of your hospital stay and ask him to get you in touch with the other medical Erasmus students at the hospital. I didn't do that, but I wish that I had, because I met some great friends far too late in my internship.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language! Very few people speak english, and since my spanish wasn't that good it was challenging and sometimes quite lonely, but still I always managed in the end.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The lifestyle is very chill and people are very nice. Gijón is an amazing town, with great seafood, sidewalk cafés and a big beach with many dogs!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
If in doubt don't waste your time trying to figure things out yourself, just ask. 
Try the specialities you find interesting and try to ask if you can go with the same doctor most of the time. I really enjoyed the opportunity of getting to know people better that way and not just being another random student every day. 
If you want to try a procedure or to do the medical examination, you usually can, so don't be afraid to ask

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I bought a used bike for 150 euro and sold it again for 75 euros when I left. I can really recommend it! It seemed like a lot of money at first, but I really loved my route to the hospital each day and having the opportunity to go for trips in the weekend. I think that it actually saved me money in the end, since I didn't take the bus at any time.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing another culture and learning that even though your danish guidelines tells you treat one way, it is not the only right way to treat a patient - that was a very interesting perspective for me. Also I got the opportunity to examine things I haven't done before like a neck-back-stiffnes, a large abdominal tumor, splenomegaly and listening to many hearts and lungs with my stethoscope

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language again. Most doctors were very kind, spoke great english and really tried to explain, but I also met some doctors who didn't even wanted to try to explain to me in english, and I lost a lot of important information this way. Also I wasn't really able to speak to patients, but when I was with the kind doctors it wasn't really a problem, and sometimes I was with a local medical student or a resident, who would explain things to me.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I began learning Spanish a year before my trip, so if you want to go, but don't speak spanish yet, don't let it stop you! Even though it was challenging for me sometimes, both taking evening classes before and not being able to understand everything, I had an amazing trip and would really recommend it. Gijón is also an amazing place so it is a win-win!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
